The tide comes in twice a day along most coasts, pulled by the moon and, to a smaller degree, by the sun. When the two line up, the water climbs higher than usual and falls lower too. Fishermen watch these spring tides closely, because a channel that is deep at noon can be a stretch of wet sand by evening.

A loaf of bread begins with four plain things: flour, water, salt and yeast. Kneading stretches the dough until it turns smooth and springy. Left in a warm place, it slowly swells as the yeast breathes out tiny bubbles of gas. A hot oven sets the crust, and the kitchen fills with a smell that is hard to resist.

Bicycle chains wear out more quickly than most riders expect. Grit mixes with oil and grinds against the links, so the chain stretches a little each month. A stretched chain skips on the teeth of the rear gears. Wiping it with a rag and adding a few drops of fresh oil every couple of weeks keeps the whole drive running quietly.

On a clear night far from town lights, the band of the Milky Way can be seen arching across the sky. It is the edge-on view of our own galaxy, made of more stars than anyone could count. Binoculars show that the faint haze is really countless points of light, packed so closely that the eye blends them together.

The old railway station had a tall clock above the main hall, and travellers set their watches by it. Pigeons nested in the iron beams of the roof. In the mornings the platforms filled with people carrying coffee and newspapers, and the announcements echoed off the tiled walls long after each train had pulled away.

Tomatoes grow best with plenty of sun and steady watering. Uneven watering can split the fruit or leave dark patches at the bottom. Gardeners often tie the stems to wooden stakes so the heavy branches do not snap. By late summer the plants can reach shoulder height, and the ripe fruit comes in faster than one household can eat.

Rivers rarely run in straight lines. Water flows faster on the outside of a bend, wearing away the bank, while slower water on the inside drops sand and gravel. Over many years the bends grow wider and drift across the valley floor. Sometimes a loop is cut off entirely and left behind as a curved lake.

A small public library on a weekday afternoon is a quiet place. A few students work at the long tables, an older man reads the newspaper by the window, and a child sits on the carpet with a picture book. The librarian sorts returned books onto a trolley and wheels them, one shelf at a time, back to where they belong.

Honey keeps for a very long time because it holds so little water that bacteria cannot grow in it. Bees make it from the nectar of flowers, fanning their wings to dry it before sealing each cell with wax. The colour and taste change with the flowers nearby, so honey from clover is pale and mild while honey from heather is dark and strong.

Snow forms high in the clouds when water vapour freezes onto tiny specks of dust. Each crystal grows six arms as it falls, and the exact shape depends on the temperature and moisture it meets on the way down. Fresh snow is mostly air, which is why it muffles sound and makes a winter street feel so still.

Market day in the square starts before sunrise, when the stall holders unload crates from their vans. By eight o'clock there are tables of apples, cheeses, eggs and bunches of flowers. People wander between the stalls with cloth bags, stopping to taste a slice of pear or to ask how a certain squash should be cooked.

Writing a letter by hand takes longer than sending a quick message, and that is part of its charm. The writer has time to choose each sentence, and the reader can see the shape of the handwriting, the crossed-out words and the little drawing in the margin. Many people keep old letters for decades in a box at the back of a drawer.
